module.title: Days 1–10 | Competition Mastery Module
module.description: Production candidate: authored topic-driven English Challenge curriculum.

lessons.title: Vocabulary in context
lessons.objective: Infer word meaning from context, word parts and contrast rather than relying only on memorised definitions.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Strong vocabulary reasoning uses the sentence and surrounding clues. Look for definition clues, examples, contrasts, tone and word parts such as prefixes and suffixes. A familiar word can have a different meaning in context, so replace the candidate meaning mentally and check whether the sentence still makes sense. Avoid choosing a synonym merely because it is broadly related.
examples: In “The path was arduous, so the hikers rested often,” the contrast with resting and the hiking context suggest that arduous means difficult or tiring.

In “The path was arduous, so the hikers rested often,” the contrast with resting and the hiking context suggest that arduous means difficult or tiring. Apply the same reasoning to a new sentence or passage and require the learner to explain why the selected answer fits.
lessons.practical_activity: Underline the clue words in five sentences and infer the meaning of one unfamiliar word in each.
lessons.guided_practice: Work through three scaffolded English problems for Vocabulary in context: model the first, prompt the second, and require independent justification on the third. Require the learner to point to the word, sentence or relationship supporting the answer.
independent_practice: Choose the best meaning from context
Identify the clue supporting the answer
Use a prefix or suffix to narrow a word's meaning
Distinguish a precise synonym from a merely related word.
lessons.assessment_checkpoint: Complete an eight-item vocabulary checkpoint and justify at least six choices with contextual evidence.
lessons.student_task: Build a personal vocabulary table with word, inferred meaning, clue and original sentence.
lessons.tutor_guidance: Prompt learners to identify the exact textual or grammatical evidence before confirming an answer. When an option is wrong, explain the distractor pattern rather than only naming the correct option. The sequence is also suitable for self-learning.
lessons.reflection_completion: Explain one case where the dictionary meaning of a word would not be the best answer in context.
lessons.daily_flow: Learn → Worked Example → Guided Practice → Independent Practice → Check → Reflect

lessons.title: Grammar and sentence structure
lessons.objective: Identify grammatical relationships and select forms that make sentences clear, precise and internally consistent.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Grammar questions become easier when the learner identifies the subject, verb, modifiers and relationships before choosing an option. Check subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, pronoun reference, articles, prepositions and parallel structure. Prefer the option that preserves the intended meaning while remaining grammatically complete.
examples: “Neither the teacher nor the students were late” requires attention to the subject closest to the verb and to the intended agreement pattern.

“Neither the teacher nor the students were late” requires attention to the subject closest to the verb and to the intended agreement pattern. Apply the same reasoning to a new sentence or passage and require the learner to explain why the selected answer fits.
lessons.practical_activity: Mark the subject and main verb in six sentences, then diagnose one grammar error in each.
lessons.guided_practice: Work through three scaffolded English problems for Grammar and sentence structure: model the first, prompt the second, and require independent justification on the third. Require the learner to point to the word, sentence or relationship supporting the answer.
independent_practice: Correct agreement errors
Choose consistent verb tense
Repair unclear pronoun references
Identify the complete subject and predicate
Fix a broken parallel construction.
lessons.assessment_checkpoint: Complete an eight-item grammar checkpoint with at least six correct and an explanation for each correction.
lessons.student_task: Write five sentences deliberately containing different grammar issues, then edit them accurately.
lessons.tutor_guidance: Prompt learners to identify the exact textual or grammatical evidence before confirming an answer. When an option is wrong, explain the distractor pattern rather than only naming the correct option. The sequence is also suitable for self-learning.
lessons.reflection_completion: Identify the grammatical rule behind your most difficult correction rather than memorising the corrected sentence.

lessons.title: Reading comprehension and main idea
lessons.objective: Identify the central idea, supporting details and purpose of a passage without confusing a detail with the author's main point.
lessons.core_teaching_content: A main idea is the controlling message of a passage, while supporting details explain, illustrate or qualify it. Read for the overall purpose before selecting an answer. Eliminate options that are too narrow, too broad or contradicted by the passage. A strong answer should be supportable from the text.
examples: If a passage describes several ways a community reduces waste, the main idea is likely the broader approach to waste reduction rather than one recycling method.

If a passage describes several ways a community reduces waste, the main idea is likely the broader approach to waste reduction rather than one recycling method. Apply the same reasoning to a new sentence or passage and require the learner to explain why the selected answer fits.
lessons.practical_activity: Read a short passage, write its main idea in one sentence, then classify each detail as supporting, secondary or irrelevant.
lessons.guided_practice: Work through three scaffolded English problems for Reading comprehension and main idea: model the first, prompt the second, and require independent justification on the third. Require the learner to point to the word, sentence or relationship supporting the answer.
independent_practice: Choose the best title
Identify the central claim
Match details to the claim
Eliminate an answer that is true but too narrow.
lessons.assessment_checkpoint: Complete an eight-item comprehension checkpoint with evidence for at least six answers.
lessons.student_task: Write a one-sentence summary and cite two details that support it.
lessons.tutor_guidance: Prompt learners to identify the exact textual or grammatical evidence before confirming an answer. When an option is wrong, explain the distractor pattern rather than only naming the correct option. The sequence is also suitable for self-learning.
lessons.reflection_completion: Explain why one true statement from the passage can still be a poor main-idea answer.
lessons.daily_flow: Learn → Worked Example → Guided Practice → Independent Practice → Check → Reflect

lessons.title: Inference and evidence
lessons.objective: Make reasonable inferences that extend beyond explicit wording while remaining anchored to textual evidence.
lessons.core_teaching_content: An inference combines what the text says with what can reasonably be concluded. It is not a guess based on outside assumptions. Separate explicit facts from inferred conclusions and ask which sentence or detail supports the inference. Strong options are usually the least speculative conclusion that explains the evidence.
examples: If a character checks the dark sky, carries an umbrella and hurries home, it is reasonable to infer that rain may be expected, but not that the character definitely knows the exact forecast.

If a character checks the dark sky, carries an umbrella and hurries home, it is reasonable to infer that rain may be expected, but not that the character definitely knows the exact forecast. Apply the same reasoning to a new sentence or passage and require the learner to explain why the selected answer fits.
lessons.practical_activity: For each short passage, write one explicit fact and one supported inference, then identify the evidence for the inference.
lessons.guided_practice: Work through three scaffolded English problems for Inference and evidence: model the first, prompt the second, and require independent justification on the third. Require the learner to point to the word, sentence or relationship supporting the answer.
independent_practice: Distinguish fact from inference
Select the inference best supported by two clues
Reject an option that adds an unsupported assumption
Identify the evidence sentence.
lessons.assessment_checkpoint: Complete an eight-item inference checkpoint and cite textual evidence for at least six answers.
lessons.student_task: Write a claim-evidence pair from a short passage without adding unsupported details.
lessons.tutor_guidance: Prompt learners to identify the exact textual or grammatical evidence before confirming an answer. When an option is wrong, explain the distractor pattern rather than only naming the correct option. The sequence is also suitable for self-learning.
lessons.reflection_completion: Describe one inference that would be too speculative and explain what evidence is missing.

lessons.title: Sequence, cause and effect
lessons.objective: Trace events and ideas in logical order and distinguish direct causes, contributing factors and consequences.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Sequence questions test relationships rather than simple memory. Look for time markers, transitions and logical dependencies. Cause and effect should be separated: an event can contribute to an outcome without being its only cause. Words such as because, therefore, before, after, consequently and however often signal relationships.
examples: A project may be delayed because materials arrive late; the late delivery is a cause, while the missed deadline is a consequence.

A project may be delayed because materials arrive late; the late delivery is a cause, while the missed deadline is a consequence. Apply the same reasoning to a new sentence or passage and require the learner to explain why the selected answer fits.
lessons.practical_activity: Reorder five mixed statements into a coherent sequence and draw one cause-effect chain.
lessons.guided_practice: Work through three scaffolded English problems for Sequence, cause and effect: model the first, prompt the second, and require independent justification on the third. Require the learner to point to the word, sentence or relationship supporting the answer.
independent_practice: Identify the first and final event
Find a missing step
Match causes to effects
Distinguish a direct cause from a later consequence.
lessons.assessment_checkpoint: Complete an eight-item sequence and cause-effect checkpoint with at least six correct relationships.
lessons.student_task: Create a six-step process and label two causal links.
lessons.tutor_guidance: Prompt learners to identify the exact textual or grammatical evidence before confirming an answer. When an option is wrong, explain the distractor pattern rather than only naming the correct option. The sequence is also suitable for self-learning.
lessons.reflection_completion: Explain why chronological order and causal order are not always identical.

lessons.title: Word relationships and analogies
lessons.objective: Solve analogies and word relationships by identifying the exact relationship rather than matching surface similarity.
lessons.core_teaching_content: An analogy may express function, category, part-to-whole, degree, cause-effect, location, tool-user or other relationships. First state the relationship in words, then test the answer choices against that relationship. A visually or semantically similar word is not sufficient if the relationship differs.
examples: “Thermometer is to temperature as scale is to weight” expresses an instrument-to-measurement relationship.

“Thermometer is to temperature as scale is to weight” expresses an instrument-to-measurement relationship. Apply the same reasoning to a new sentence or passage and require the learner to explain why the selected answer fits.
lessons.practical_activity: Classify ten word pairs by relationship type before solving new analogies.
lessons.guided_practice: Work through three scaffolded English problems for Word relationships and analogies: model the first, prompt the second, and require independent justification on the third. Require the learner to point to the word, sentence or relationship supporting the answer.
independent_practice: State the relationship between the first pair
Test each option using the same relationship
Reject a pair that shares vocabulary but not structure
Create one valid analogy.
lessons.assessment_checkpoint: Complete an eight-item analogy checkpoint and explain the relationship for each answer.
lessons.student_task: Create four original analogies using four different relationship types.
lessons.tutor_guidance: Prompt learners to identify the exact textual or grammatical evidence before confirming an answer. When an option is wrong, explain the distractor pattern rather than only naming the correct option. The sequence is also suitable for self-learning.
lessons.reflection_completion: Identify why one tempting analogy option matches the topic but not the relationship.

lessons.title: Editing, punctuation and precision
lessons.objective: Edit sentences for clarity, punctuation, concision and standard written usage while preserving intended meaning.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Editing requires reading the whole sentence rather than reacting to one word. Check commas, apostrophes, sentence boundaries, modifiers and unnecessary repetition. Precision means choosing wording that communicates the intended relationship without ambiguity. When two options are grammatically acceptable, use meaning, clarity and economy to decide.
examples: “After finishing the report, Maya submitted it” has a clear modifier; moving the opening phrase can accidentally imply that the report performed the action.

“After finishing the report, Maya submitted it” has a clear modifier; moving the opening phrase can accidentally imply that the report performed the action. Apply the same reasoning to a new sentence or passage and require the learner to explain why the selected answer fits.
lessons.practical_activity: Edit a short paragraph in two passes: first for correctness, then for clarity and concision.
lessons.guided_practice: Work through three scaffolded English problems for Editing, punctuation and precision: model the first, prompt the second, and require independent justification on the third. Require the learner to point to the word, sentence or relationship supporting the answer.
independent_practice: Repair a comma splice
Correct an apostrophe
Remove redundant wording
Fix an ambiguous modifier
Choose the clearest sentence among grammatically acceptable options.
lessons.assessment_checkpoint: Complete an eight-item editing checkpoint with at least six correct corrections.
lessons.student_task: Rewrite a 100-word paragraph for clarity without changing its meaning.
lessons.tutor_guidance: Prompt learners to identify the exact textual or grammatical evidence before confirming an answer. When an option is wrong, explain the distractor pattern rather than only naming the correct option. The sequence is also suitable for self-learning.
lessons.reflection_completion: Identify one edit that improves clarity rather than merely correcting a grammar rule.

lessons.title: Evidence-based written response
lessons.objective: Construct concise answers that make a claim, support it with relevant evidence and explain the connection.
lessons.core_teaching_content: A strong response answers the exact question, selects relevant evidence and explains why that evidence matters. Avoid copying a long passage without interpretation. For short responses, a claim-evidence-explanation structure is often enough. The best evidence is specific and directly connected to the question.
examples: For a question about a character's decision, quote or paraphrase the action that demonstrates the decision and explain how it supports the interpretation.

For a question about a character's decision, quote or paraphrase the action that demonstrates the decision and explain how it supports the interpretation. Apply the same reasoning to a new sentence or passage and require the learner to explain why the selected answer fits.
lessons.practical_activity: Write a three-sentence response to a short passage: answer, evidence, explanation. Then remove one irrelevant detail.
lessons.guided_practice: Work through three scaffolded English problems for Evidence-based written response: model the first, prompt the second, and require independent justification on the third. Require the learner to point to the word, sentence or relationship supporting the answer.
independent_practice: Identify the claim in a model response
Select the strongest evidence
Explain the evidence
Rewrite an answer that is accurate but insufficiently supported.
lessons.assessment_checkpoint: Complete an eight-item evidence checkpoint and ensure every response has a defensible textual basis.
lessons.student_task: Produce one polished short response using claim, evidence and explanation.
lessons.tutor_guidance: Prompt learners to identify the exact textual or grammatical evidence before confirming an answer. When an option is wrong, explain the distractor pattern rather than only naming the correct option. The sequence is also suitable for self-learning.
lessons.reflection_completion: Circle the sentence in your response that actually explains why the evidence supports your claim.

lessons.title: Speed, distractors and integrated mini-mock
lessons.objective: Apply vocabulary, grammar, comprehension and reasoning strategies under time pressure while controlling common distractor errors.
lessons.core_teaching_content: Competitive English tests reward accuracy first and speed second. Read the question stem carefully, predict what kind of answer is required, eliminate clearly wrong options, and return to the passage when evidence matters. Common distractors may be true but irrelevant, grammatically attractive but meaningfully wrong, too extreme or unsupported by the text. After a timed set, classify mistakes to improve the next attempt.
examples: A comprehension option may repeat a sentence from the passage but fail to answer the actual question; factual truth alone does not make it correct.

A comprehension option may repeat a sentence from the passage but fail to answer the actual question; factual truth alone does not make it correct. Apply the same reasoning to a new sentence or passage and require the learner to explain why the selected answer fits.
lessons.practical_activity: Complete a mixed timed set, mark uncertain questions, then review errors by category rather than simply counting the score.
lessons.guided_practice: Work through three scaffolded English problems for Speed, distractors and integrated mini-mock: model the first, prompt the second, and require independent justification on the third. Require the learner to point to the word, sentence or relationship supporting the answer.
independent_practice: Solve one vocabulary item, one grammar item, one inference item, one analogy and one evidence question
For every missed item, identify the distractor type.
lessons.assessment_checkpoint: Complete an integrated checkpoint and record accuracy, time, guessed items and error categories.
lessons.student_task: Create a one-page English Challenge revision plan with three strengths, three gaps and one measurable next-attempt target.
lessons.tutor_guidance: Prompt learners to identify the exact textual or grammatical evidence before confirming an answer. When an option is wrong, explain the distractor pattern rather than only naming the correct option. The sequence is also suitable for self-learning.
lessons.reflection_completion: State which error pattern cost the most marks and the specific strategy you will use to reduce it.
